transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-08-07 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SE), Liam (Helix Platform), Sana (Helix ML infra), Arjun (CTO), Marta (Helix Security)
---
Auto-generated summary: deep dive on tail latency and network hops; some transcription mistakes likely

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick agenda — we want to figure out why your p95/p99 spikes on inference and whether streaming or non-streaming mode helps given your robotics control loop. Diego will run through latency traces and batching options.

[00:18] Liam: yeah, thanks. high-level — we're running a mix of short chatty prompts (20-80 tokens) and some long planning prompts (~800 tokens) for mission planning. our SLOs are 150ms p95 and 350ms p99 for the short path, longer ones are higher tolerance but still concerned about worst-case tails.

[00:35] Diego: got it. a couple of clarifying q's — what GPUs are you using today, and are you on-prem or cloud?

[00:42] Sana: currently we have a hybrid setup. the training cluster is GCP (A100), inference is mostly on-prem Triton-ish boxes with RTX6000 class cards. we also have a small burst pool in a cloud region.

[00:58] Priya: important to note — the on-prem boxes are behind a NAT and a firewall, and there are two network hops to the control plane for telemetry. Marta, any security callouts?

[01:06] Marta: our auditors require KMS-backed keys for payload encryption and SOC2 log retention. we prefer private control plane or VPC peering; don't want customer data leaving our VPC.

[01:20] Diego: great, that's helpful. at a high level, tail latency usually comes from three buckets: kernel execution variance (model pathing + KV cache misses), batching-induced queuing, and network hop variability (especially TCP handshakes and transient routing).

[01:33] Arjun: can you explain KV cache behavior again? we expected it to dramatically reduce p99 but see mixed results.

[01:40] Diego: sure — our runtime supports prefix and key-value cache that caches past KV tensors for autoregressive decoding. when you have high reuse (many requests with shared prefixes), hit rate is high and per-token compute drops. two caveats — cache lookup cost and cache eviction can introduce jitter. if you have many unique prefixes, the cache hit falls and you pay the full kernel cost which increases p95/p99. also note the network path to where KV cache is stored matters if it's remote.

[02:05] Liam: we're seeing p99 spikes specifically on bursts during fleet-wide firmware updates — lots of simultaneous short requests that don't share prefixes.

[02:16] Diego: that's a classic cold-KV problem. strategies: 1) client-side prefix coalescing or pre-warming, 2) prioritize low-latency routing for small requests (route to hot pool), 3) adjust batching thresholds to avoid long wait times for p95-sensitive paths.

[02:34] Priya: about batching — we've seen in testing that aggressive batching reduces cost but increases 99th percentile. what's the recommendation?

[02:40] Diego: right, batching trades cost for latency. Redwood supports dynamic batching with latency caps. you can set a max wait threshold (e.g., 5ms) and a max batch size. for your short-control-path, we'd recommend small batch windows and a smaller max batch. for background planning requests, allow bigger batches. the runtime also supports continuous batching which can help by smoothing but still maintain tail SLOs if you set per-route latency caps.

[03:05] Sana: what about streaming vs non-streaming? some of our control flow needs streaming partial tokens while others use full-response non-streaming. we saw weird p99 behavior in streaming mode during network blips.

[03:15] Diego: streaming adds additional network round trips — you commit an initial response chunk, then more chunks follow. If you have packet loss or a hop that adds variance, streaming p99 can worsen because each chunk adds another exposure. For short single-chunk responses streaming is usually fine, but for many small chunks or flaky networks, non-streaming single-payloads can be more predictable. Also the server-side flush policy and connection keepalive settings matter a lot.

[03:42] Arjun: is there a way to combine both — like stream locally and batch on the backend?

[03:48] Diego: yes — edge aggregation is a pattern: do partial assembly at a nearby edge node and send fewer aggregated requests to the heavy on-prem GPU. That reduces network hops and KV misses. It requires an edge component but for robotics that often pays off.

[04:03] Liam: can we talk quantization? we tested int8 and int4 and saw reduced latency but worse variance for some sequences.

[04:12] Diego: quantization reduces kernel compute but can change kernel selection. int4 (4-bit) gains are model-dependent; some attention kernels are less stable and can cause longer jit fallback times or different memory access patterns which sometimes increases p99 on long sequences. int8 often is a safer middle-ground. Also pay attention to per-layer quantization sensitivity; mixed-precision (select layers int8, others fp16) helps. the runtime will avoid slow fallback kernels if you pin a quantization profile, but that can increase base latency.

[04:45] Sana: you mentioned kernel selection and JIT — how does Redwood pick kernels? we saw logs referencing triton/kern-42 names that we didn't recognize.

[04:52] Diego: the compilation layer benchmarks kernels against sequence-length distributions and picks the fastest kernel per op for your hardware. if the sequence length or batch size distribution shifts, the chosen kernel might be suboptimal, leading to variance. we log kernel choices and perf numbers — Diego: we'll share an export of those kernel logs.

[05:10] Arjun: network detail — we have two NAT hops and an internal LB that terminates TLS. where do you think the biggest variance comes from?

[05:18] Priya: likely the LB and NAT. ephemeral port exhaustion or uneven connection reuse can introduce latency bursts. also TLS handshake reuse matters; if connections are not reused you pay CPU and handshake delays. our recommendation: persistent connections, regional peering, or private control plane to minimize public internet hops.

[05:37] Marta: security wise, will private control plane satisfy SOC2 and our KMS requirements? we can't have tokens stored unencrypted.

[05:44] Maya: yes — Redwood Private supports bring-your-own-kms (BYOK), HSM integrations, and audit log exports. we also support VPC peering and private endpoints so no public egress required. we'll share the security top-level deck and our SOC2 report.

[06:02] Liam: can you walk through an example trace? we prepared a p99 trace sample (attached in the meeting notes).

[06:10] Diego: reading trace — I see a 220ms kernel time, 80ms waiting in queue, and intermittent 40-60ms on TCP retransmit. The KV cache miss path adds the 220ms; on hit you'd be ~60ms kernel time. So the miss multiplier is the big factor for p99.

[06:35] Sana: is the 80ms batching queue from our client or yours? we instrumented client that enqueues requests for batching at 50ms — could be compounding.

[06:42] Diego: exactly — both sides can enqueue. client-side coalescing plus server-side dynamic batching can interact. we recommend centralizing batching policy in the runtime with client hints to avoid double-queueing.

[06:56] Arjun: what observability do we need to identify these components?

[07:02] Priya: you should collect per-request trace id, timestamps at client send, server receive, kernel start/end, KV cache hit/miss, batch size, and network time. Redwood Console can ingest these and break down p95/p99 by bucket. Diego: we'll send a sample tracing spec and a small shim to emit these fields.

[07:24] Liam: for the pilot, will Redwood run a canary with our on-prem boxes or do we need to stage in our cloud burst pool?

[07:31] Maya: both options are possible. for on-prem we do a private control plane integration and can run a dedicated pool to minimize interference. for initial benchmarking we can use your cloud burst pool to get faster iteration.

[07:45] Marta: any legal/contract concerns for on-prem connectivity? we prefer not to allow inbound control-plane initiated connections into our private subnet.

[07:53] Priya: we support outbound-only control plane connections via an agent; that satisfies most air-gapped policies. we'll include that in the checklist.

[08:05] Diego: a few quick recommendations from what I see: 1) separate low-latency route (no batching or tiny batch cap) for control messages, 2) pre-warm KV cache for critical prefixes using a cheap bulk pre-warm job, 3) use mixed precision (int8 + fp16) initially rather than int4 for stability, 4) implement edge aggregation for fleets with many small requests.

[08:25] Sana: can we see the throughput/cost tradeoffs for those changes? we have strict power constraints on edge nodes.

[08:33] Diego: yes — our Redwood Optimize module can run simulated workloads and produce token-cost curves vs latency. we'll run a scenario comparing int8 vs int4 and small batch vs large batch and return a simple cost-latency plot.

[08:50] Liam: about instrumentation — Diego, you said you'll provide the kernel logs. do you need anything special from our side?

[08:57] Diego: helpful to have a span ID mapping and sample payloads. also we need a copy of your sequence-length distribution and burst profile (which you said you'd share).

[09:05] Maya: recap — Diego will create deterministic bench and share configs; Priya will send VPC/on-prem checklist and security notes; Liam will export histograms and p95/p99 samples; we'll plan a follow-up on 2025-08-18 for network topology.

[09:20] Arjun: timeline looks good. one last q: any immediate low-effort wins to reduce p99 today?

[09:25] Diego: yes — reduce client-side batching windows, enable persistent connections/keepalive, pin int8 quant profile, and route critical control to hot pool. Also add a small pre-warm job for top 200 prefixes. Those are low-effort and often cut p99 by 30-50% in practice.

[09:45] Marta: please send security docs and SOC2.

[09:48] Maya: will do.

[09:50] Meeting close, agreed action items and owners repeated.
